answer.sourceLine: Washington said it in his First Annual Address to Both Houses of Congress, delivered at Federal Hall in New York City on 8 January 1790 — the message we now call the State of the Union. The sentence appears verbatim in the address, immediately after he asks Congress to give “providing for the common defence” particular regard.

8 January 1790 — Federal Hall, New York City

source.excerpt: To be prepared for war is one of the most effectual means of preserving peace. A free people ought not only to be armed, but disciplined; to which end a uniform and well-digested plan is requisite; and their safety and interest require that they should promote such manufactories as tend to render them independent of others for essential, particularly military, supplies.
trail: Primary text. The sentence stands verbatim in Yale's Avalon Project transcript of the First Annual Message ↗, dated 8 January 1790.
Independent transcription. The American Presidency Project ↗ prints the same sentence, dated January 8, 1790, followed immediately by the “free people ought not only to be armed” passage.
Reference confirmation. Wikiquote lists it among Washington's sourced 1790s quotations ↗, cited to “First Annual Address, to both Houses of Congress (8 January 1790).”

Earlier English parallel. Gibbon had already written of the Romans that “They preserved peace by a constant preparation for war” in Chapter I of the Decline and Fall ↗ — the same thought in near-identical English, predating Washington's address.

author.name: George Washington

author.metaLine: 1732–1799 · Commander of the Continental Army · First President of the United States
author.bio: George Washington commanded the Continental Army through the Revolutionary War, presided over the Constitutional Convention, and served two terms as the first President of the United States. He had spent eight years watching a part-time militia go short of powder, muskets and discipline, and the experience shaped almost everything he later said about defense. His 1790 address to Congress — still the shortest State of the Union on record — is where that hard-won view got its most quotable sentence.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is sound — the trouble is the wording, the sentence next door, and the assumption that Washington thought of it first.

items.why: Washington wrote effectual. The modernised “most effective means of preserving peace” circulates widely — it has run as a military quote of the day with “effective” in the headline ↗. Same meaning, not his word.

A viral quote runs: “A free people ought not only be armed and disciplined, but they should have sufficient arms and ammunition to maintain a status of independence from any who might attempt to abuse them, which would include their own government.” Only the opening words are Washington's — they come from the sentence directly after this one in the same 1790 address, and the rest is invented. PolitiFact rated it Mostly False ↗.

Washington coined the sentence, not the thought. The Roman writer Vegetius had written Igitur qui desiderat pacem, praeparet bellum, later condensed into the motto si vis pacem, para bellum — an idea traced to the fourth or fifth century AD ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is real, and it is Washington's: it stands word for word in the First Annual Address of 8 January 1790 ↗ — with “effectual,” and without the extra clause about one's own government.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Washington delivered this address at Federal Hall in New York City on 8 January 1790, and the National Archives notes it “remains the shortest one ever” — the briefest State of the Union in American history ↗. In a message that short, every sentence is doing work, and this one opens the section on national defense.

The point he was actually pressing was industrial, not rhetorical. The very next sentences ask Congress to fund a disciplined militia under “a uniform and well-digested plan” and to promote domestic manufactories so the country would not depend on foreign suppliers for muskets and powder — the shortage that had nearly broken the Continental Army under his own command.
detailsBody: The thought was old long before 1790. The Roman writer Vegetius had put it as Igitur qui desiderat pacem, praeparet bellum — “let him who desires peace prepare for war” — a line later smoothed into the motto si vis pacem, para bellum (Wikipedia ↗).

Nearly the same sentence exists in English in Edward Gibbon's Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, Chapter I, describing the Antonine emperors: “They preserved peace by a constant preparation for war” (full chapter text ↗). Washington's phrasing is his own; the idea behind it was already centuries old.
context.pull: The shortest State of the Union ever given, and this is the line that survived it.
